newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Inflow fails to end Slovak liquidity crunch.
newsitem.headline: Inflow fails to end Slovak liquidity crunch.

text.p: Fresh liquidity from strong foreign currency sales flowed into the Slovak interbank money market on Thursday, but dealers warned the market still faced an acute shortage of funds.
They said that heavy foreign currency selling by local and foreign banks had by Thursday afternoon pushed interbank rates down by up to 70 basis points to between 21.5 and 26 percent.
But dealers cautioned that the market was having difficulty digesting the new funds.

"The inflow may not necessarily help to relax the crunch as the interbank credit lines are a big problem. To place a 25 million crown package has become difficult," Martin Tatar, a dealer at ING Bank told Reuters.

Patrik Banary of Slovenska Sporitelna added: "Even if placed, the flows from abroad may leave the market as quickly as they come, either due to a deposit rate decline or adversity of the central bank foreign exchange rate policy".

The banking sector has become highly illiquid since the central bank stopped quoting securities repo and reverse repo rates at the beginning of the year, instead holding tenders when needed for limited volumes of short-term securities repos.
The move is the latest effort by the National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) to rein in a rapidly growing money supply and cool off a consumption-led boom.
"Liquidity is flowing in the sector from abroad, and within three days the liquidity situation may improve," said Martin Hrozany, chief dealer at savings bank Slovenska Sporitelna.

But the moves also have increased pressure on smaller banks to raise prime lending rates, threatening them with the loss of their few lucrative clients, a problem exacerbated by the fact that even large Slovak companies rely mainly on short-term rollover loans to finance their operations.

Several local banks failed to fulfil Wednesday's minimum reserve requirements, and banks' crown buying pushed the sector's accumulated reserves down to 10.32 percent below the minimum, despite Thursday's flow of funds.

The country's leading banks were forced earlier this week to cut by a half minimum compulsory traded volumes for one month to hedge against the interest rate volatility, though they still kept quotation spreads unchanged at one percent.

The NBS has warned banks they should raise interbank credit lines again, or its limited refinancing volumes will be of no use. It added that there is no need at this point to change their current policy, since the moves were hitting the target,
Many banks, however, said they still hoped that the NBS would either reverse the recent moves.
"The line is a risk of the partner, and the tendency now is rather to switch to reciprocity," Peter Sandor, a Ponobanka dealer, said.

"If liquidity continues to crunch, some of the banks below minimum reserves are likely to have difficulties with settlements since the emergency credit institute no longer exists," a liquidity expert with a foreign bank said.
The NBS cancelled the emergency credit, which allowed banks in an emergency to get debt at the clearing centre, a year ago.
Thursday's strong crown purchases prompted the central bank to fix the crown at 80 basis points below the dollar/mark basket midpoint on Thursday, after fixing it at 1.4 percent below on Wednesday.
By late afternoon, the crown had strengthened and was 0.05 percent above the basket midpoint.
